claim: Sensory systems discard redundant information through adaptation to the mean and variance of the environment to maximize information transmission.
source: To maximize information transmission, sensory systems discard redundant information through adaptation to the mean and variance of the environment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle of sensory systems, drawing on established scientific knowledge about efficient coding.

claim: Larval fruit flies adapt sensory-motor computations underlying navigation to changes in the variance of visual and olfactory inputs.
source: Here, we study how larval fruit flies adapt sensory-motor computations underlying navigation to changes in the variance of visual and olfactory inputs.
evidence: This is the main research question stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Variance adaptation in larval fruit flies can be characterized by rescaling of the sensory input.
source: We show that variance adaptation can be characterized by rescaling of the sensory input
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 2, where input rescaling better describes the adaptation than output rescaling.

claim: For both visual and olfactory inputs, the temporal dynamics of adaptation are consistent with optimal variance estimation.
source: for both visual and olfactory inputs, the temporal dynamics of adaptation are consistent with optimal variance estimation.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison with Bayesian optimal estimators shown in Figure 6.

claim: In multisensory contexts, larvae adapt independently to variance in each sense.
source: In multisensory contexts, larvae adapt independently to variance in each sense
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments in Figure 7 where only the stimulus with changing variance shows adaptation.

claim: Portions of the navigational pathway encoding mixed odor and light signals are capable of variance adaptation.
source: portions of the navigational pathway encoding mixed odor and light signals are also capable of variance adaptation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 bottom row, where correlated stimuli with changing combined variance show adaptation.

claim: Multiplication is a mechanism for odor-light integration in larval fruit flies.
source: Our results suggest multiplication as a mechanism for odor-light integration.
evidence: This is inferred from the multisensory variance adaptation experiments and reanalysis of previous data, as shown in Figure 8.

claim: Nervous systems must respond appropriately in varied environments while obeying biophysical constraints and minimizing energy expenditure.
source: Nervous systems must respond appropriately in varied environments while obeying biophysical constraints and minimizing energy expenditure (Niven and Laughlin, 2008).
evidence: This is a general principle cited from the literature.

claim: Sensory systems use strategies at all levels of organization to detect and transmit relevant information about the world to the rest of the brain, often operating near the limits imposed by their physical properties.
source: Sensory systems use strategies at all levels of organization, from sub-cellular to network-level structures, to detect and transmit relevant information about the world to the rest of the brain, often operating near the limits imposed by their physical properties (Bialek, 1987; Niven and Laughlin, 2008).
evidence: This is a general principle cited from the literature.

claim: One strategy to maximize the conveyance of sensory information is to reduce redundancy by filtering out predictable portions of sensory inputs.
source: One strategy to maximize the conveyance of sensory information is to reduce redundancy by filtering out predictable portions of sensory inputs (Barlow, 1961; Attneave, 1954; Srinivasan et al., 1982).
evidence: This is a principle from information theory cited from the literature.

claim: Responses of large monopolar cells of the blowfly retina to intensity changes were found to be optimally matched to the range of stimuli encountered in the fly's natural environment.
source: Early evidence of efficiency in the way sensory neurons encode environmental information was found in the large monopolar cells of the blowfly retina, whose responses to intensity changes were found to be optimally matched to the range of stimuli encountered in the fly's natural environment (Laughlin, 1981).
evidence: This is a historical finding cited from the literature.

claim: When environmental conditions change, neurons' coding must adapt to the new environment's statistics to maintain an efficient representation of the world.
source: If neurons' responses are indeed tuned to a specific environmental distribution of inputs, then when environmental conditions change, the neurons' coding must adapt to the new environment's statistics to maintain an efficient representation of the world (Tkačik and Bialek, 2016; Maravall, 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical principle cited from the literature.

claim: Variance adaptation has been measured across diverse organisms in visual, auditory, olfactory, and mechanosensory systems and in deeper brain regions.
source: Variance adaptation has been measured across diverse organisms in visual, auditory, olfactory, and mechanosensory systems and in deeper brain regions (Brenner et al., 2000; Fairhall et al., 2001; Kvale and Schreiner, 2004; Dean et al., 2005; Nagel and Doupe, 2006; Dahmen et al., 2010; Maravall et al., 2007; De Baene et al., 2007; Wen et al., 2009; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Clemens et al., 2018; Smirnakis et al., 1997; Gollisch and Meister, 2010; Clifford et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2016; Kim and Rieke, 2001)
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Variance adaptation in blowfly H1 neurons maximized information transmission.
source: Classic experiments in blowfly H1 neurons showed that variance adaptation in the firing rate maximized information transmission (Brenner et al., 2000; Fairhall et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a classic finding cited from the literature.

claim: In rhesus monkeys performing an eye pursuit task, adaptation to variance was observed in both the firing rates of MT neurons and in the ultimate eye movements.
source: In rhesus monkeys performing an eye pursuit task (Liu et al., 2016), adaptation to variance was observed in both the firing rates of MT neurons, maximizing information transmission, and in the ultimate eye movements, minimizing tracking errors, showing that efficiency in neural coding has observable effects on behavioral responses.
evidence: This is a finding cited from the literature.

claim: Drosophila larvae move in a series of relatively straight runs interspersed with reorienting turns.
source: Drosophila larvae move in a series of relatively straight runs interspersed with reorienting turns.
evidence: This is an established observation about larval locomotion.

claim: A key element of the larva's navigational strategy is the decision to turn, that is to cease forward movement and execute a reorientation maneuver to select a new direction for the next run.
source: A key element of the larva's navigational strategy is the decision to turn, that is to cease forward movement and execute a reorientation maneuver to select a new direction for the next run.
evidence: This describes the behavioral element being studied.

claim: The larva's decision to turn can be modeled as the output of a Linear-Nonlinear-Poisson (LNP) cascade and characterized through reverse correlation.
source: This decision can be modeled as the output of a Linear-Nonlinear-Poisson (LNP) cascade and characterized through reverse correlation (Gepner et al., 2015; Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015; Aljadeff et al., 2016; Parnas et al., 2013; Schwartz et al., 2006; Chichilnisky, 2001).
evidence: This is a methodological approach cited from the literature.

claim: For both visual and fictive olfactory stimuli, the scaled turn-triggered averages were nearly identical at low and high variance.
source: We found that for both visual and fictive olfactory stimuli, the scaled turn-triggered averages were nearly identical at low and high variance (Figure 1d)
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: At low variance, the turn-triggered averages had a slightly longer 'shoulder' 3–4 s prior to the eventual turn.
source: although at low variance, the averages had a slightly longer 'shoulder' 3–4 s prior to the eventual turn.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: For both visual and fictive olfactory stimuli the rate function was steeper at low variance than high variance, indicating a more sensitive response to the same input in the low variance context.
source: We found that for both visual and fictive olfactory stimuli the rate function (Figure 1e) was steeper at low variance than high variance, indicating a more sensitive response to the same input in the low variance context.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Rate functions calculated using variance-specific filters were nearly identical to those found using a single shared kernel.
source: These rate functions were nearly identical to those we found using a single shared kernel.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: An input rescaling far better described the adaptation than an output rescaling.
source: We found that an input rescaling far better described the adaptation than an output rescaling
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model comparison in Figure 2a,d using BIC values.

claim: The high and low variance rate functions have the same non-zero output at zero stimulus input.
source: a straightforward consequence of the high and low variance rate functions having the same non-zero output at zero stimulus input.
evidence: This is inferred from the rate functions shown in Figure 1e and Figure 2.

claim: The input rescaling model was better at predicting held out data than either output rescaling model, in the aggregate and on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: we found that the input rescaling model was better at predicting held out data than either output rescaling model, in the aggregate (Figure 2b,e) and on a trial-by-trial basis (Figure 2c,f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the jackknife analysis shown in Figure 2b,c,e,f.

claim: For all sensory inputs tested (visual, Or42a, Or42b, Or59a, Or35a, Gr21a), the linear filters were nearly the same at high and low variances.
source: We found that in all cases, the linear filters were nearly the same at high and low variances
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3a for multiple genotypes.

claim: For all sensory inputs tested, the slope of the nonlinear rate function adapted to variance.
source: and that the slope of the nonlinear rate function adapted to variance (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3b for multiple genotypes.

claim: For all inputs, the scaling factor decreased suddenly following a step increase in variance but increased more gradually following a step decrease.
source: We found that for all inputs this scaling factor decreased suddenly following a step increase in variance but increased more gradually following a step decrease.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c for multiple genotypes.

claim: The asymmetric temporal dynamics of adaptation are consistent with the response of an optimal variance estimator.
source: This is consistent with the response of an optimal variance estimator (DeWeese and Zador, 1998).
evidence: This is inferred by comparison with theoretical predictions from cited work.

claim: Larvae adapt to variance using a stimulus with uncorrelated random values.
source: The linear filter, found as the mean subtracted and scaled turn-triggered average, encoded the same temporal dynamics at low and high variance (Figure 4a). The nonlinear rate function was steeper in the low variance condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b) indicating variance adaptation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 using a different stimulus type.

claim: With uncorrelated random value stimuli, larvae showed faster adaptation to an increase in variance than a decrease.
source: We then examined the temporal dynamics of adaptation using a stimulus whose variance switched every 20 s (in analogy to Figure 3) and found a faster adaptation to an increase in variance than a decrease (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The larva's adaptation to environmental variance is consistent with an optimal estimate of that variance and indicates an input sampling rate of ~ 1.2–1.5 Hz.
source: Thus, the larva's adaptation to environmental variance is consistent with an optimal estimate of that variance and indicates an input sampling rate of ~ 1.2–1.5 Hz.
evidence: This is inferred from the best-fit Δt values found in the Bayesian estimator analysis.

claim: Only the response to the switching stimulus adapted, while for the fixed-variance stimulus, the turn-rate remained constant.
source: We found that only the response to the switching stimulus adapted, while for the fixed-variance stimulus, the turn-rate remained constant (Figure 7)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 for multisensory experiments.

claim: Variance adaptation is accomplished on a uni-sensory basis and prior to multi-sensory combination.
source: indicating that variance adaptation is accomplished on a uni-sensory basis and prior to multi-sensory combination.
evidence: This is inferred from the multisensory experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Elements of the navigational circuit that have access to both light and odor inputs have the ability to adapt to variance.
source: This adaptation must be implemented by circuit elements that have access to both light and odor inputs, showing that elements of the navigational circuit well downstream of the sensory periphery also have the ability to adapt to variance.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlated stimulus experiments shown in Figure 7 bottom row.

claim: Larvae linearly combine odor and light stimuli to make navigational decisions.
source: We previously found that larvae linearly combine odor and light stimuli to make navigational decisions (Gepner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: Variance adaptation in larvae requires a form that preserves linearity.
source: Taken together, these results require a form of variance adaptation that preserves linearity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of unisensory variance adaptation and linear multisensory integration.

claim: There is no evidence of competing pathways encoding opposite polarities in the larva's olfactory system.
source: Rectified signals encoding opposite polarities can be combined to produce a linear response (Werblin, 2010; Molnar et al., 2009), but there is no evidence of such competing pathways in the larva's olfactory system.
evidence: This is stated based on knowledge of the larval olfactory system.

claim: The adult fly adapts to variance beginning in the olfactory receptor neurons themselves.
source: The adult fly adapts to variance beginning in the olfactory receptor neurons themselves (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a finding cited from the literature.

claim: The multiplicative model produced a statistically significantly better fit to the multisensory data than did the early linear combination model.
source: we found that for both white noise (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and step experiments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), the multiplicative model produced a statistically significantly better fit to the data than did the early linear combination model, even after accounting for the different number of model parameters.
evidence: This is shown by the reanalysis of previous data in Figure 8 supplements.

claim: The multiplicative model better predicted held-out data than the early linear combination model.
source: The multiplicative model also better predicted held-out data.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1c.

claim: When larvae were presented with white noise visual stimuli in a fluctuating CO₂ background, the visual response was insensitive to the magnitude of the fluctuations.
source: Indeed, when we presented larvae with white noise visual stimuli in a fluctuating CO2 background, we found that the visual response was insensitive to the magnitude of the fluctuations (Figure 9b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9b.

claim: The convolution kernels for visual and fictive olfactory stimuli have very similar shapes.
source: In LNP model fits to the reverse-correlation experiments, we found that the convolution kernels for visual and fictive olfactory stimuli have very similar shapes
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 3a.

claim: Both visual and olfactory stimuli are low passed to the same temporal resolution.
source: suggesting that both visual and olfactory stimuli are low passed to the same temporal resolution (Gepner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar kernel shapes and cited from previous work.

claim: The decision to cease a run and end a turn is a navigational response to stimulus changes generated by larva's movement through the environment.
source: The decision to cease a run and end a turn is a navigational response to stimulus changes generated by larva's movement through the environment.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about the nature of the behavior being studied.

claim: For navigational decisions, the larva should seek sensory input that changes at the frequency of its own peristaltic movement.
source: For this decision, the larva should seek sensory input that changes at the frequency of its own peristaltic movement, and this time scale should be the same for light and odor.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about optimal sensory processing for navigation.

claim: Electrophysiological and optical recordings in olfactory sensory neurons reveal that these neurons filter odor inputs with similar dynamics to those observed in behavioral reverse correlation experiments.
source: Indeed, electrophysiological (Schulze et al., 2015; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017) and optical (Si et al., 2017) recordings in olfactory sensory neurons reveal that these neurons filter odor inputs with similar dynamics to those observed in our behavioral reverse correlation experiments.
evidence: This is cited from the literature to support the interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: If light and odor were sampled at different rates, we would expect different rates of adaptation following a switch to low variance.
source: If light and odor were sampled at different rates, we would expect different rates of adaptation following a switch to low variance.
evidence: This is a logical prediction used to interpret the data.

claim: The same rates of adaptation for both light and odor suggest that sensory input is filtered to match the frequency of the larva's own motion.
source: In fact, we see the same rates of adaptation for both light and odor, and these rates are consistent with an optimal estimator sampling the stimulus at a similar frequency to the bandwidth of the convolution kernels. These suggest that sensory input is indeed filtered to match the frequency of the larva's own motion.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of adaptation rates across modalities.

claim: If the bandwidth of the filter kernels is set by the speed of the larva's own motion and not the temporal dynamics of the environment per se, this would explain why the temporal structures of the kernels do not adapt to changes in variance.
source: If the bandwidth of the filter kernels is set by the speed of the larva's own motion and not the temporal dynamics of the environment per se, this would also explain why the temporal structures of the kernels do not adapt to changes in variance (Figure 1d, Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed lack of kernel adaptation.
